content: The term concomitant drugs is used in two distinct contexts: in medicine and in drug abuse. Concomitant Drugs in Medicine In the medical field, the term concomitant drugs refers to the administration of two or more medicinal drugs either simultaneously or within a short time frame, such as one after the other or on the same day. This practice is common in medical treatments. For example, in the adjuvant treatment of stage III colon cancer, the standard of care involves chemotherapy protocols such as FOLFOX (used in Europe, Japan, Canada, and Australia) or FLOX (used in the USA). These protocols are fundamentally similar and consist of three drugs: a) Leucovorin (also known as folinic acid or calcium folinate), b) 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU), and c) Oxaliplatin. These three drugs are considered concomitant because they are administered together as part of the treatment regimen. Another example involves the use of iodinated contrast media in imaging procedures such as X-rays, CT scans, or MRIs. While these contrast agents are essential for diagnostic purposes, they are known to cause acute allergic reactions in some patients and can also lead to kidney damage. Radiologists, therefore, take precautions by inquiring about other medications the patient may be taking concomitantly before the imaging procedure. They often monitor kidney function and hydration status, especially if the patient is using other drugs that may harm the kidneys. Concomitant Drugs in Drug Abuse In the context of drug abuse, concomitant drugs refers to the use of two or more substances of misuse either at the same time or within a short time frame, such as one after the other or on the same day. This practice has been studied to determine its impact on mortality rates. For instance, research conducted in Sheffield, UK, analyzed whether the concomitant use of drugs, such as an opiate combined with another substance of misuse, increases the number of accidental opiate-related deaths. The findings indicated that intravenous (IV) administration of opiates was the most consistent factor associated with drug-related deaths in the Sheffield area. The co-administration of another concomitant drug of misuse was observed as a common feature in these deaths but was not identified as an independent risk factor. Notes 1.
